How much would Bitcoin need to be worth to match the real purchasing power of $1 million from different eras?

The equivalent of $1 million in 2023 purchasing power would require Bitcoin to reach roughly $1.5 million per BTC (around 2036), while matching the purchasing power of $1 million in 1983 would require a price of approximately $6 million per BTC (around 2043). 

In other words, simply becoming a "Bitcoin millionaire" will gradually mean less as inflation erodes the value of money. To preserve the purchasing power of a historical $1 million, Bitcoin would ultimately need to trade well above the $1 million mark.

📌 Zcash sets July 28 hard fork to seal Orchard after critical bug 

⚠️ Zcash founder Zooko Wilcox has explained how the network’s July 28 Ironwood hard fork will address uncertainty around a critical flaw in the Orchard shielded pool. The upgrade will not identify or freeze individual counterfeit coins. Instead, it will seal the old pool and limit how much ZEC can leave. 

🔖 Ironwood, also known as NU6.3, is scheduled to activate at block 3,428,143 on July 28. The upgrade will retire the current Orchard pool and introduce a new shielded pool based on the corrected circuit. According to Zcash’s official Ironwood user update, users will no longer be able to send or receive ZEC inside the old Orchard pool after activation. Funds can leave only through the turnstile, which prevents more ZEC from exiting than legitimately entered.

⭐️ The Zcash team said it believes the flaw was “unlikely to have been exploited,” but users cannot independently prove no counterfeit ZEC was created. Ironwood aims to trap any excess value inside the old pool rather than allow it to enter wider circulation. Security researcher Taylor Hornby discovered the Orchard flaw on May 29 while auditing the shielded system. The bug could have allowed an attacker to create counterfeit ZEC inside Orchard without leaving an obvious public record.

If salvation can be forfeited, then at some point its security depends on my continued performance.

That raises a question Scripture never answers.

How much faithfulness is enough?

How much obedience is enough?

How much sin is too much?

The Bible never gives us such a standard because our assurance was never meant to rest on our performance.

It rests on God’s promises.

One final thought.

Repentance does not make us perfect.

It never has.

King David is a wonderful example.

After his terrible sins of adultery and murder, he cried out to God in repentance.

Read Psalm 51.

There you will find not the prayer of a perfect man, but the cry of a broken sinner who cast himself entirely upon the mercy of God.

David did not claim perfection.

He confessed his sin, acknowledged his guilt, and threw himself upon the mercy of God.

That is what genuine repentance looks like.

Repentance is not sinless perfection.

It is the broken heart of a sinner who recognizes his need for a perfect Savior.

Believers are not sinless.

But as they walk with the Lord, by the power of the Holy Spirit, they should sin less - not to remain saved, but because they have been saved.

The Father chose you.

The Son redeemed you.

The Holy Spirit sealed you.

The same God who has faithfully preserved Israel for thousands of years despite her repeated failures is the God who faithfully preserves every person who has been born again through faith in Yeshua.

Our confidence is not in the strength of our grip on God.

Our confidence is in the strength of His grip on us.

God’s faithfulness has never been performance-based.

It has always been based on who He is.
